entries.clue: Ruin atmosphere following devilish child (6)

indicatorNotes.following: Something following another thing is written after it, so the atmosphere is set down behind the child rather than in front.

blocks.note: an imp is a small mischievous demon, the crossword's standing naughty infant
the air is the atmosphere around us

annotation.surface: A mood that trails around after a badly behaved youngster.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruin atmosphere' wants to read as one phrase, the child spoiling the mood; only the first word is the definition and it is a verb. The two halves then sit in clue order reversed by 'following'.
annotation.definitionFit: To impair something is to damage or weaken it — impaired hearing, impaired judgement — the sense of ruin that stops short of destroying outright.

entries.clue: Agitated Welshmen lose a food delivery (5,2,6)

indicatorNotes.Agitated: Something agitated has been shaken out of the order it was in, so the letters beside it are to be rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

annotation.surface: Welshmen in a state about having mislaid something.
annotation.walkthrough: Everything but the last two words is fodder, which is why the middle of the clue reads like nothing anybody would say. 'Lose' looks like an instruction to drop letters and is only more raw material.
annotation.definitionFit: Meals on Wheels is the British service that drives hot dinners round to housebound people — food delivery, long before anyone used the phrase.

entries.clue: Calm destruction of sausage! (7)

indicatorNotes.destruction of: Destruction leaves a thing in pieces, and letters in pieces can be put back together in any order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: An outraged cry at a sausage being wrecked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Calm' has to be the verb here, the one you do to somebody else's fears, not the adjective the surface suggests. Seven letters of fodder for a seven-letter answer says nothing is being added or dropped.
annotation.definitionFit: To assuage grief, guilt or hunger is to soothe it and take the edge off — calm used as a verb rather than a description.

entries.clue: Artist has bit of fierce competition (3,4)

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the letters a painter puts after their name
a bit of something left behind is a trace of it

annotation.surface: A painter with a streak of ruthless rivalry in him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bit of' is nearly always the instruction to take a first letter, and here it is not: the short word is wanted whole for its meaning, and 'of' merely joins wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The rat race is the grinding scramble for money and advancement among people all chasing the same jobs — competition at its least pleasant.

entries.clue: Leaves ring in maritime game (6)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the piece named before it inside the piece named after it, rather than alongside.

blocks.note: somebody who leaves a job quits it
a ring is drawn as the round letter

annotation.surface: Foliage encircling something out at sea.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' invites the plural noun and is the third-person verb, which is why it has an S to lose the ring into. Deck quoits — rope rings thrown at a peg — was the standard amusement on liners.
annotation.definitionFit: Quoits is the ring-throwing game, played on ship decks with rope hoops, which is why a setter can call it maritime.

entries.clue: Allotment appears in part of misquotation (5)

indicatorNotes.part of: A part of a word is a stretch of its letters taken as they come, so the answer is sitting inside the word named.

blocks.note: the letters stand unbroken inside the word, starting at its fourth

annotation.surface: A ration turning up inside a garbled version of somebody's words.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters never cross a word boundary, which is the harder version of this trick — the eye reads a long word as one shape and skips what is inside it. 'Allotment' is the share doled out, not the vegetable patch.
annotation.definitionFit: A quota is the fixed share assigned to someone — an import quota, a sales quota — which is what an allotment of anything means.

entries.clue: Different parent heading off (5)

indicatorNotes.heading off: Heading off reads as leaving, and taken apart it says the head comes off: the word loses the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: a mother is a parent, and the word gives up its first letter

annotation.surface: A parent setting out on a journey.
annotation.walkthrough: One letter is the whole operation, so the clue lives or dies on spotting which parent is meant — the other one would leave nothing usable. 'Heading off' does double duty as departure and as decapitation.
annotation.definitionFit: The other one is the different one, the one that is not this — take the other road, some other day.

entries.clue: Pass a critical point round the bend (4,3,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition describes the manoeuvre instead of naming it — to go round the bend is to do this — which a double definition allows when the phrase has no noun form.

blocks.note: the moment in an illness, a slump or a crisis after which things start improving
the plain physical act of driving or walking round a curve in the road

annotation.surface: Getting past the dangerous stretch just beyond the curve in the road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round the bend' is British slang for insane, and that sense is the trap — the clue wants the literal curve in the road. Thirteen letters split (4,3,6) leaves very little room for anything but two definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: A patient or an economy that turns the corner is past the worst of it, and taken literally the phrase is simply going round a bend.

entries.clue: Loud singing voice restraining composed singing voice (8)

indicatorNotes.restraining: To restrain something is to hold it and not let it out, so the word doing the restraining closes around the other.

blocks.note: f is forte on a score, the musician's mark for loud
the alto is the voice between soprano and tenor
somebody composed is set, calm and settled

annotation.surface: A booming voice keeping a calmer one under control.
annotation.walkthrough: The same two words are the wordplay's raw material and the definition, sitting at opposite ends of the clue — a deliberate echo, not a slip. 'Composed' offers the writing of music and means self-possessed.
annotation.definitionFit: A falsetto is the high register a man sings in above his natural range, so it names a singing voice as directly as alto does.

entries.clue: Cows listened to audibly (4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Cows' is plural and the answer a singular collective; setters freely let the group noun stand for the animals in it.

indicatorNotes.audibly: Audibly means out loud, so the words beside it are wanted for their noise and not for their spelling.

blocks.note: something listened to has been heard, and that word said aloud can be written another way

annotation.surface: Cattle being made out clearly from somewhere across the field.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cows' reads first as the verb meaning intimidates, which is a dead end. A homophone this short turns on one swapped vowel pair, so the crossings matter more than usual.
annotation.definitionFit: A herd is the word for cattle taken together — a herd of cows — so the animals and their collective noun answer for each other.

entries.clue: Largest continent part of the Bahamas, I assume (4)

indicatorNotes.part of: Part of something is a piece of it exactly as it stands, so consecutive letters of the words that follow are what is wanted.

blocks.note: the run starts at the sixth letter of the islands and finishes on the first letter of the last word

annotation.surface: Guessing which scatter of islands belongs to the Bahamas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Part of' reads as a geographical claim and works as an extraction instruction, which is what holds the surface together. The letters cross a comma and two word breaks, exactly where the eye slides past.
annotation.definitionFit: Asia is the biggest continent by both area and population, so the superlative picks it out on its own.

entries.clue: Short review covered by a song's briskness (8)

indicatorNotes.covered by: What is covered by something has that thing over the top of it, so the first piece goes inside the second.

blocks.note: a lay is a song, the minstrel's word, and the possessive ending only joins the wordplay to the definition
a crit is a review, the trade's own clipping of criticism

annotation.surface: A brief write-up buried somewhere in the quickness of a song.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lay' for song is the crossword's favourite scrap of old vocabulary, kept alive by setters needing three easy letters. 'Short' governs 'review' rather than telling you to drop a letter from something else.
annotation.definitionFit: Alacrity is brisk, willing speed — she accepted with alacrity — so briskness names the quality without the eagerness.

entries.clue: Building extension where woman embraces former partner (6)

indicatorNotes.embraces: To embrace somebody is to put your arms right round them, so the word doing it closes over the other.

blocks.note: Anne is the setter's standby woman, four letters and a name everyone knows
an ex is the partner you used to have

annotation.surface: An extra wing of a building being used as the spot for a reunion with an old flame.
annotation.walkthrough: The old flame goes inside the woman rather than after her, which is what 'embraces' insists on. The final E is the British spelling of the building; American English drops it.
annotation.definitionFit: An annexe is the subsidiary block put up beside or onto a main building — a school annexe, a hotel annexe — which is a building extension.

entries.clue: Butterflies discovered in cleaner vests (6)

indicatorNotes.discovered in: Discovered in says the answer is already sitting inside the words that follow, to be read off as they stand.

blocks.note: the run begins at the fourth letter of the first word and finishes inside the second

annotation.surface: Insects found among the fresher of the vests in a drawer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Butterflies' looks like the subject of a sentence about laundry and is the definition, pointing at the stomach rather than the wardrobe. The comparative 'cleaner' is there only to keep the surface upright while the letters run across the gap.
annotation.definitionFit: Butterflies in the stomach are what people call the jitters before an exam or a speech, which is the same thing as nerves.

entries.clue: Out of the running at present in this place (7)

blocks.note: at present means now
in this place means here

annotation.surface: A competitor with no chance at the moment, at least at this venue.
annotation.walkthrough: Two everyday adverbs laid end to end, and the join is invisible because both halves are so plain that neither looks like a piece. The definition is the racing sense: a horse that comes nowhere finishes outside the placings.
annotation.definitionFit: A runner or candidate who finishes nowhere was never in contention, which is what being out of the running means.

entries.clue: Sappers gave up – retreated (7)

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's diggers and bridge-builders, known as sappers
a country that gave up territory ceded it

annotation.surface: Army engineers who surrendered and then pulled back.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash does the work a link word would, separating the building instructions from the meaning. Sappers are worth learning as two letters: they turn up in Guardian and Metro puzzles alike.
annotation.definitionFit: A tide, a hairline or an army that receded moved back from where it had been, which is what retreated says.

entries.clue: Cutting tool was china, broken (8)

indicatorNotes.broken: Broken china is in pieces on the floor, and letters in pieces can be swept back together in any order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Something that used to be a decent dinner service and is now smashed.
annotation.walkthrough: The indicator is the last word of the clue and belongs to the crockery on the surface, which is why the break reads so naturally. 'Was' is fodder rather than the sentence's verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A chainsaw is the petrol-driven saw used to fell trees and cut logs, a cutting tool in the most literal sense there is.

entries.clue: In Paris, Sue's the point in question (5)

indicatorNotes.In: In says the answer is already inside the words that follow, to be read straight off without reordering them.

blocks.note: the run starts at the fourth letter of the city and carries on through the name

annotation.surface: Explaining that in Paris it is Sue who matters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' almost always announces a French word, and that is the trap — here 'in' is plain English telling you to look inside. The apostrophe-s is part of the hiding place, not a possessive to unpack.
annotation.definitionFit: The issue is the matter under dispute — the real issue here, to take issue with someone — which is the point in question.

entries.clue: Create a lead in tennis (3,2)

annotation.definitionNote: The tennis half is a scoreline read aloud — a player a set up is one set ahead — so it is a phrase rather than a noun the answer could replace.

blocks.note: the sense of founding or establishing — a company, a committee, an experiment in a laboratory
being one set ahead of the opponent, as commentary phrases a scoreline in a match

annotation.surface: Building an advantage in the middle of a tennis match.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration (3,2) is the tell that two short words are wanted, and 'Create' on its own at the front is the shape a double definition always takes. Tennis commentary says a player is a set up the way darts says one leg up.
annotation.definitionFit: To set something up is to create or establish it, and in tennis to be a set up is to be one set ahead of the opponent.

entries.clue: Company fine for Delia Smith, eg (4)

blocks.note: co is the abbreviation on every firm's letterhead
fine as an answer to how are you means OK

annotation.surface: A firm's penalty being charged to a well-known television presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine' offers the penalty a company might pay and means the everyday agreement instead, which is the whole trap. 'Eg' flags Delia Smith as one instance of the word wanted rather than the word itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Delia Smith is the British television cook whose recipe books taught a generation to boil an egg, so she is one example of a cook.

entries.clue: Touches headless fish (4)

indicatorNotes.headless: Headless means without a head, so the word it governs loses the letter standing at its front.

blocks.note: somebody who touches a fabric feels it, and the word drops its first letter

annotation.surface: Somebody handling fish that have had their heads taken off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Headless' attaches to the fish on the surface and to the first word underneath, and that switch is the only difficulty in four letters. Fish is the same word singular and plural, so the enumeration gives nothing away.
annotation.definitionFit: Eels are the long snake-like fish of rivers and estuaries, so the bare plural 'fish' covers them without further description.

entries.clue: Walking to unusual gradient (8)

indicatorNotes.unusual: What is unusual is not in its normal state, and letters out of their normal state are letters out of their normal order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Strolling towards an oddly steep slope.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words do three different jobs in a row, which is why 'to unusual gradient' reads as one phrase. The definition has to stay a participle so that it can be swapped for the answer in a sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Treading is walking with the weight of the foot in it — treading carefully, treading water, treading the boards.

entries.clue: Resting general bitten by snake (6)

indicatorNotes.bitten by: What is bitten by something has been taken into its jaws, so it ends up inside the creature named.

blocks.note: the asp is Cleopatra's snake and the shortest one a setter can use
Robert E. Lee commanded the Confederate army, and three letters make him the setter's default general

annotation.surface: A commanding officer bitten by a snake while he takes a break.
annotation.walkthrough: 'General' offers the adjective meaning widespread before it settles into a rank, and the rank turns out to be one particular man. The snake does the containing, so the general goes inside rather than after.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody asleep is at rest, and the two words swap straight across in a sentence about a dog in front of the fire.

entries.clue: Shipyard workers head off with senior people (6)

indicatorNotes.head off: Head off reads as setting out on a journey, and taken literally it says the head comes off: the first letter goes.

blocks.note: welders join the steel plates a hull is built from, the trade the Clyde and Tyne yards ran on, and the word loses its first letter

annotation.surface: Dockyard tradesmen setting out somewhere in the company of their seniors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head off' means departure on the surface and beheading underneath, which is the one joke in the clue. Naming the trade rather than the place is what makes the long word findable.
annotation.definitionFit: Elders are the senior figures of a village or a church, the people whose years give them authority over the rest.
